opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, that period in Singapore was really my first real taste of what research actually is. Before that, as an undergrad, I had a kind of romantic, vague idea about it: you read papers, you have ideas, and somehow things work out. At NUS I got thrown into an environment where people were actually doing it every day, submitting to top conferences, running experiments late at night, arguing about results. That changed how I saw things.

I think the biggest gain wasn't any specific paper or technique. It was a sense of taste and pace. I saw how a working lab operates: how you go from a rough idea to something you can test, how quickly you need to iterate, and how often your first intuition turns out to be wrong. Computer vision was changing very fast then, and being close to that, even as a junior person, gave me a feel for which problems seemed exciting versus which were incremental.

It also gave me confidence. When you're young and coming from a place where research feels distant, you don't really know if you can do it. Having people there who took my ideas seriously, who would sit down and debug with me or push back on my thinking, made me feel this was something I could pursue as a career, not just a side interest.

And honestly, there was a lot of frustration too. Many things I tried didn't work. But I think learning to live with that, accepting that most experiments fail and that's normal, was probably one of the most valuable lessons. That mindset carried into my PhD and everything after.

So if I had to sum it up, NUS was where I went from being curious about research to really wanting to become a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response describes gaining a practical understanding of research through lab experience and experimentation, but it does not say that writing a research paper creates a substantially different understanding from never having written one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing I got from that time in Singapore was a kind of grounding before I went to graduate school. I was still an undergraduate, and I didn't yet have a clear sense of what research actually looked like day to day. At that point I knew I liked computer vision, but mostly through courses and reading papers, which is a very different thing from sitting in a lab and trying to make something work.

So the first gain was just experience: learning how to take a vague idea, turn it into an experiment, fail, debug, and try again. That loop sounds simple, but you have to go through it yourself to understand it. Nobody can teach you the feeling of running something for a week and realizing the baseline was wrong. I went through that early, and it made the beginning of my PhD much less painful.

The second thing was mentorship. The people I worked with there were very generous with their time, and they treated me as a collaborator rather than just a student doing tasks. That shaped how I think about advising now. I try to give students real problems and real ownership, because that's what helped me.

And the third thing, honestly, was confidence and perspective. Singapore is a very international place, and the lab had people from all over Asia and beyond. It was the first time I felt that research is a global conversation, not something that happens only in a few famous places. That made it easier for me later to move to the US, to work in industry, and then come back to academia. I stopped thinking of any one environment as the center of everything, and I think that mindset has served me well.

r001.rationale: The response says that doing experiments, debugging, and retrying taught the speaker what research is like, but it does not mention writing a research paper or compare that experience with never having written one.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, the biggest thing I gained was a sense of what it means to do research. When you’re taking classes, the problem is usually well defined, and you expect there to be an answer. In research, you first have to figure out what the right question is, and then accept that your first few ideas may not work.

That experience also helped me understand my own interests. It wasn’t just about learning techniques or completing a project; it was about discovering whether I enjoyed that process of exploring something uncertain. I think that was especially valuable early on—it gave me a clearer sense that research was something I wanted to keep pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning to frame uncertain research questions and discovering an interest in research, but it does not mention writing a research paper or contrast that experience with never having written one.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think the biggest thing I gained was a clearer sense of what research actually involves. You start with a question, try something, and often discover that your assumptions were wrong. Learning to work through that uncertainty—to understand why an experiment failed and decide what to try next—was very valuable. It also helped me figure out whether I enjoyed the process of research, beyond just getting a good result.
